'''''Syncarpia glomulifera''''', commonly known as the '''turpentine tree''', or '''yanderra''',<ref>{{NSW GNR|id = SXlpZxtLuj|title = Yanderra}}</ref> is a tree of the family [[Myrtaceae]] native to [[New South Wales]] and [[Queensland]] in Australia, which can reach {{convert|60|m|ft|abbr=off}} in height. It generally grows on heavier soils. The cream flowers appear in spring and are fused into compound flowerheads.

==Taxonomy==
English botanist [[James Edward Smith (botanist)|James Edward Smith]] first described the turpentine as ''Metrosideros glomulifera'' in 1797, from a collection in the Sydney district.<ref name=apniold>{{APNI | name = ''Metrosideros glomulifera'' Sm. | id = 56859}}</ref> It was given its current binomial name by German botanist [[Franz Josef Niedenzu]] in 1893.<ref name=apni>{{APNI | name = ''Syncarpia glomulifera'' (Sm.) Nied. | id = 9355}}</ref> Common names include turpentine, luster, red turpentine or red luster.<ref name=apni/> It was formerly known as ''Syncarpia laurifolia'' Ten.<ref name=EJ10>{{cite book |author1=Elliot, Rodger W. |author2=Jones, David L. |author3=Blake, Trevor |title=Encyclopaedia of Australian Plants Suitable for Cultivation: Volume 9 – Sp-Z|year=2010 |publisher=Lothian Press |location=Port Melbourne |isbn=978-0-7344-0974-4|page=159}}</ref> Two subspecies are recognised, the widespread nominate, and subspecies ''glabra'' which is found from [[Bulahdelah, New South Wales|Bulahdelah]] north to [[Kempsey, New South Wales|Kempsey]] and has smooth leaf undersurfaces.<ref name="Boland"/>

==Description==
In a suitable location, the turpentine grows into a large straight-trunked tree up to 45 or even 55 m (150–180 ft) high with a [[Diameter at breast height|DBH]] of up to 1.3 or even 1.5 m (4–5 ft).<ref name="Boland">{{cite book|author1=Boland, Douglas J. |author2=Brooker, M. I. H. |author3=Chippendale, G. M. |author4=McDonald, Maurice William |title=Forest trees of Australia|publisher=CSIRO Publishing|location=Collingwood, Victoria|year=2006|pages=628|isbn=0-643-06969-0|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=q2v3kb9tFsYC&q=%22Syncarpia+glomulifera%22&pg=PA628}}</ref> On poorer soils it grows as a small tree or even adopts a [[Mallee (habit)|mallee]] habit.<ref name=Ben98>{{cite journal |last=Benson |first=Doug |author2=McDougall, Lyn  |year=1998|title=Ecology of Sydney plant species:Part 6 Dicotyledon family Myrtaceae |journal=Cunninghamia |volume=5 |issue=4 |pages=809–987 |url=http://www.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0008/58049/Cun5Ben808.pdf}}</ref> The thick brown bark is fibrous, with deep vertical furrows running down the trunk. The leaves are arranged oppositely on the stems, and pairs grow close together so that they resemble a whorled group of four leaves. On 0.7–1.3 cm long [[Petiole (botany)|petiole]]s, the thick leaves are ovate to ellipictal and measure {{convert|7|–|10|cm|in|round=0.5|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|2.5|–|4.5|cm|in|round=0.5|abbr=on}} across with recurved margins. Their upper surface is a dull dark green, and lower surface much paler, either covered by fine hairs in subspecies ''glomulifera'' or smooth in ''glabra''.<ref name="Boland"/> Flowering takes place from August to December, peaking in September.<ref name=Ben98/> The cream flowers are fused in groups of seven into compound flowerheads.<ref name="Boland"/> This is followed by the development of the compound fruit – {{convert|1|to|2|cm|in||abbr=on}} diameter woody capsules which ripen in summer.<ref name=Ben98/>

==Distribution and habitat==
[[File:Turpentine Springwood Blue Mountains.jpg|thumb|left|upright|a large tree at [[Springwood, New South Wales|Springwood]], [[Blue Mountains National Park]]]]
The turpentine is found in eastern Queensland and New South Wales, from [[Atherton, Queensland|Atherton]] in the far north to as far south as [[Murramarang National Park]].<ref name="Boland"/><ref name="floransw">{{NSW Flora Online|genus=Syncarpia |species=glomulifera|author=Wilson, Peter G.}}</ref> North of [[Gympie]], the distribution is fragmented, with colonies on the [[Blackdown Tableland National Park|Blackdown]] and [[Consuelo Tableland]]s, [[Tinaroo, Queensland|Tinaroo]] district and [[Windsor Tableland]].<ref name="Boland"/> The habitat most commonly associated with the turpentine is transitional forest between rainforest and wet sclerophyll forest.<ref name="Boland"/> Here it grows as an [[Rainforest#Emergent layer|emergent]] tree,<ref name="floransw"/> and is associated with such trees as flooded gum (''[[Eucalyptus grandis]]''), tallowwood (''[[Eucalyptus microcorys|E. microcorys]]''), grey ironbark (''[[Eucalyptus paniculata|E. paniculata]]''), white stringybark (''[[Eucalyptus globoidea|E. globoidea]]''), yellow stringybark (''[[Eucalyptus muelleriana|E. muelleriana]]''), white-topped box (''[[Eucalyptus quadrangulata|E. quadrangulata]]''), rough-barked apple (''[[Angophora floribunda]]''), brush box (''[[Lophostemon confertus]]'') and various rainforest species.<ref name="Boland"/><ref name=Ben98/> It also grows with spotted gum (''[[Corymbia maculata]]'') and blackbutt (''[[Eucalyptus pilularis|E. pilularis]]'').<ref name="Boland"/> On poorer soils, it can grow much smaller in dry sclerophyll forest in association with smooth-barked apple (''[[Angophora costata]]'') and yellow bloodwood (''[[Corymbia eximia]]'').<ref name=Ben98/>

Adaptable to a wide range of soils, the turpentine is most suited to moderate to high-nutrient soils, such as clay soil over [[Wianamatta shale]] in the Sydney region.<ref name=Ben98/> Valleys and flat areas are highly suitable sites.<ref name="Boland"/> In the Sydney region, the species reaches an altitude of {{convert|300|m|ft|abbr=on}}, but this extends to {{convert|900|m|ft|abbr=on}} above sea level in northern Queensland.<ref name="Boland"/>

The turpentine is one of the dominant species of the critically endangered [[Sydney Turpentine-Ironbark Forest]] ecological community.<ref name=Ben98/>

The largest known turpentine, located near the Williams River Recreation Reserve in the [[Barrington Tops National Park]], New South Wales, measures {{convert|7.90|m|ft|0|abbr=on}} trunk circumference at breast height, {{convert|58|m|ft|abbr=on}} tall, {{convert|20|m|ft|abbr=on}} crown spread width and "points 517" (points calculated using the National Register of Big Trees formula).<ref>{{Cite web| url= https://www.nationalregisterofbigtrees.com.au/listing_view.php?listing_id=878 | title= Turpentine. ''Syncarpia glomulifera''. Measured by Don Cruickshanks, October, 2013 | work= National Register of Big Trees Australia | access-date= 27 Nov 2013}}</ref>
{{Clear|left}}

==Ecology==
The flowers are pollinated by native bees and European honeybees, and possibly flies and moths. The [[grey-headed flying fox]] (''Pteropus poliocephalus'') and [[little red flying fox]] (''P. scapulatus'') also pollinate the flowers. The [[rainbow lorikeet]] (''Trichoglossus haematodus'') and [[noisy miner]] (''Manorina melanocephala'') forage for nectar.<ref name=Ben98/>

The turpentine regenerates after bushfire by resprouting from its [[lignotuber]] and [[epicormic bud]]s. Turpentine trees are thought to live up to 500 years.<ref name=Ben98/>

==Uses==
Highly durable, turpentine timber is used in heavy-traffic flooring, for poles and wharves. It resists marine invertebrates and termites, and is one of the most difficult timbers to ignite.<ref name="Boland"/> A hardy and adaptable tree, turpentine tolerates heavy soils and frosts, and is suitable for large gardens and parks, where it provides good shade with its dense canopy.<ref name=EJ10/>
